The Langmuir isotherm describes adsorption onto a fixed number of equivalent, non-interacting sites, relating fractional coverage to gas partial pressure through an equilibrium constant. Because the equilibrium constant is tied to a free energy of adsorption, fitting measured coverages yields thermodynamic quantities that can be used to predict coverage at other temperatures and pressures; deviations from the model signal site heterogeneity or adsorbate-adsorbate interactions.

## Single-site model for CO2 capture on supported amidines (2010)

Alesi et al. used a single-site, two-component Langmuir form in which CO2 and H2O react together at an amidine site to form bicarbonate, with coverage taken as the measured fraction of amidines bound to CO2 ([Alesi et al. 2010](/papers/alesi2010/)). The resulting equilibrium constant gave a reaction Gibbs energy, corrected to the standard state with tabulated gas-phase data, and solving the isotherm at capture and regeneration conditions mapped out the range of reaction free energies that give useful working capacity. The model over-predicted the efficiency gain at higher CO2 pressure, which the authors suggest may come from repulsion between neighboring bicarbonates or a distribution of site energies, both violations of the Langmuir assumptions. Summary: [alesi2010](/papers/alesi2010/).
